newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU agrees to step up fight against trade in women.
newsitem.headline: EU agrees to step up fight against trade in women.

text.p: European Union ministers agreed on Saturday to step up cooperation to clamp down on the sex slave trade in women which forces hundreds of thousands into prostitution in the bloc every year.

But they stopped short of a binding commitment sought by the Dutch EU presidency to give the women -- many tricked into prostitution when seeking to flee poverty in eastern Europe -- temporary residence permits to testify against the criminals who exploit them.

The Netherlands, which organised the conference, had hoped to persuade its EU partners to embrace a system similar to its own, whereby the women are treated as victims by the police rather than illegal immigrants and deported.
With the protection of a temporary permit and police protection they can help identify and witness against their captors.
Belgium has a system similar to the Dutch and all the ministers agreed to go home and see how it could be used in their countries.
But some, including Britain and Ireland, said they had reservations as it would be difficult under their immigration laws to give the women automatic residence and protection.

The fall of the Iron Curtain left many eastern European women in financial straits, and many have been tempted into the richer EU by criminals offering them jobs as waitresses, dancers and hairdressers.

Dutch Justice Minister Winnie Sorgdrager told the conference of a 17-year-old Slovak shop assistant who was lured to the Netherlands by a 25-year-old compatriot who worked as a car smuggler. "She thought it was an adventure," Sorgdrager said.
"The police later discovered that he was in fact employed by some of the 'big boys' to recruit women for prostitution," she said.

Juergen Storbeck, chief of the EU's police agency Europol, told the conference the trade was a modern form of crime which left police forces baffled and helpless and which required a new kind of thinking among crime fighters.
"The current degree of ignorance and helplessness vis a vis modern types of crime is both astonishing and alarming...this is especially true for the trade in women and children," he said.

EU Justice Commissioner Anita Gradin, who initiated the EU's assault on trade in women in 1995, said the slave trade was "a disgrace for Europe and a tragedy for all the young women who find themselves trapped, used, and exploited".
She said that unlike trafficking in drugs, traffickers in flesh could make quick profits with little risk of being found out or prosecuted.
Despite a mounting wave of insecurity over organised crime and particularly crimes against children, EU governments have been loath to cede powers on crime fighting and immigration issues to the EU.

Even though EU ministers agreed last year that Europol should step up its role to fight trade in flesh, the vast majority of capitals have still not ratified the convention which will put it fully to work.
As a result Europol's hands are tied in the area where it could do most -- pooling and analysing information from national police forces on the trafficking.
